extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research-integrity watchers, university administrators, and science-interested public
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative considerations and debate around whether (and how) a researcher found to have fabricated data should be rehired or engaged in supporting research roles. Covers role restrictions, authorship limits, culpability of co-authors/students, evidence of reform, and institutional reputation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of suitability for research-support roles after misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether a person who fabricated data (58 retractions in this case) can be useful in a supporting/advisory role despite past misconduct; some argue 'Outside his mistake he has been a good and thorough scientist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh seriousness and scale of past fraud (retractions, legal settlement, relinquished degrees) against claimed expertise. The page records both institutional willingness to use his knowledge and public skepticism; there is no single consensus rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role restrictions as a safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional statement: 'He is not engaged in research and will not teach. He gets a supporting role, and he is the source of information and a helping hand for large projects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting duties (no direct research, no teaching) is proposed as a mitigation to reduce risk of further misconduct while still making use of domain knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on authorship or inclusion on publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment: 'As long as he can't get his name on any papers. He's affected enough co-author careers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventing the individual from being listed as co-author is suggested to protect integrity and avoid harming co-authors' reputations; this is an explicit conditional safeguard mentioned by commenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning culpability to co-authors and students
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate on whether co-authors are 'equally culpable' versus whether many co-authors were PhD students who should not be held responsible because they trusted their supervisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the roles and power differentials of collaborators; the Levelt committee (cited) is referenced as taking the position that students who trusted supervisors should not necessarily be held responsible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for demonstrable evidence of reformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Question raised: 'I'm not sure how a “fraudster” does definitively demonstrate that he or she is “reformed”.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should consider what concrete steps or evidence would indicate genuine reform (acknowledgment, remediation, oversight), since mere statements or publications about oneself may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity and scale of past misconduct as a disqualifier
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts cited about past penalties: 58 retracted papers, resignation from Tilburg University, settlement with prosecutors, 120 hours community service, relinquished PhD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the scope and legal/administrative consequences of past misconduct as factors when deciding suitability for any research-related role; commenters argue large-scale fraud may preclude any position in research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting institutional reputation and responding to staff/student concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports that the appointment was ended due to staff and student concerns; commenters note institutions must consider community reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should account for the views and safety of staff and students and may terminate engagements if trust or morale is harmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of systemic drivers (publish-or-perish) in assessing misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment: 'What remains, time and again, under the radar is the sick policy of publish or perish.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating individual cases and policy responses, also consider systemic incentives that contribute to misconduct and whether institutional reforms are needed.
